account: The Large Animal Activated Roadside Monitoring and Alert System (LAARMA) was developed by the University of Sydney's Australian Centre for Robotics and QUT's CARRS-Q. They worked with the Queensland Department of Transport and Main Roads (TMR) under an iMOVE project. It uses a machine-learning pipeline to detect large animals up to 200 m away and triggers roadside variable message signs. The ABC reported on 30 July 2025 that TMR had used the AI for three months at a busy cassowary crossing. That is on the Kennedy Highway at Kuranda, Far North Queensland. Trial dates are not given. The consortium's iMOVE project page instead describes a five-month field trial: three months of data collection, then two months of on-road trialling. The researchers report 97% recall and 77% precision, with average speed reductions of 6.30 km/h and 5.06 km/h at two zones. Their injury-risk estimates use the Nilsson model. The ABC describes a 31% fall in fatal crashes, but the inspected research summary does not establish an observed collision reduction. About two dozen cassowaries were killed on Queensland roads the previous year.

fields.account: The Large Animal Activated Roadside Monitoring and Alert System (LAARMA) was developed by the University of Sydney's Australian Centre for Robotics and QUT's CARRS-Q. They worked with the Queensland Department of Transport and Main Roads (TMR) under an iMOVE project. It uses a machine-learning pipeline to detect large animals up to 200 m away and triggers roadside variable message signs. The ABC reported on 30 July 2025 that TMR had used the AI for three months at a busy cassowary crossing. That is on the Kennedy Highway at Kuranda, Far North Queensland. Trial dates are not given. The consortium's iMOVE project page instead describes a five-month field trial: three months of data collection, then two months of on-road trialling. The researchers report 97% recall and 77% precision, with average speed reductions of 6.30 km/h and 5.06 km/h at two zones. Their injury-risk estimates use the Nilsson model. The ABC describes a 31% fall in fatal crashes, but the inspected research summary does not establish an observed collision reduction. About two dozen cassowaries were killed on Queensland roads the previous year.
